Best Rugged Tablets for Landscapers and Gardeners

13 October 2026 Tuga Hardware

For most landscapers and gardeners, the Tuga A8 is the one to look at: an 8 inch screen for quotes and plans, 1000 nits for a lawn in July, IP67 for the rain and the mud, a removable battery, and a price of £379. If the device needs to live in a pocket rather than the van, the Tuga A6 handheld at £349 is the smaller option. Whichever you choose, keep it away from the pressure washer: no device in our range is rated for jet washing.

What the Job Does to a Tablet

Landscaping is hard on electronics in a different way to construction. There is less concrete dust and a lot more of everything wet. A normal day might include:

  • Mud and grit. Soil, compost and gravel get into ports and under buttons, and wet soil carries grit into gaps and dries there.
  • Rain. Hours of it, often with the tablet face up on a wheelbarrow.
  • Sun. Open lawns with nothing to shade the screen from May to September.
  • The pressure washer. The mowers, the trailer and the tools get jet washed at the end of the day, and it is tempting to give a muddy tablet the same treatment.
  • Cold mornings. Frost, hedge cutting in January, and batteries that drop faster than they do in summer.
  • Vibration and drops. Ride on mowers, trailers, van floors, and the fall from a hip pocket when you crouch to plant.

The Specs That Matter for Garden Work

IP Rating, and the Pressure Washer Question

Start here, because it is the spec most likely to be misread. Our guide to IP68 vs IP67 covers the whole rating system. The short version for landscaping is:

  • IP68 means dust tight and able to survive immersion. Rain, mud and a brief dunk are what the rating is for. We do not list an immersion depth or time, so do not leave a device submerged. The 10.1 inch Tuga A10 is rated IP68.
  • IP67 is also dust tight and rated for immersion, to a metre for 30 minutes. The A6 and the A8 are rated IP67.
  • IP69K is a separate test for high pressure, high temperature water jets. That is the pressure washer rating. No device in our range carries it.

Neither IP67 nor IP68 covers jet washing. A pressure washer forces water past seals that would keep out a bucket of water. If it will only ever see rain, mud and the odd dunk, IP67 or IP68 covers that. Clean it with a damp cloth or a gentle rinse, not with the mowers.

One caveat: IP tests use clean, still water, and soil water and liquid feed are not. Rinse the device in fresh water after a muddy day, whatever its rating, and let it dry before you plug in a charger.

Screen Brightness

Brightness is measured in nits. A screen that is fine indoors can wash out on an open lawn in full sun, so you want a lot more. The A8 is rated at 1000 nits and listed as sunlight readable, the highest brightness figure listed in our range. No brightness figure is listed for the A6, so try it on a sunny day within the returns window. For comparison, the A10 is 350 nits, so it suits drawings in the van rather than a client meeting on a sunny patio.

Glove Mode and Wet Hands

Neither the A8 nor the A6 lists glove mode, though the A6's two side scan keys work with gloves on. Try the screen with the gloves you actually wear before relying on it. No touchscreen likes water sitting on the glass, rugged or not, so expect to wipe it on your sleeve before you tap.

Battery

Many gardens and sites have no power nearby. The A8 has an 8000mAh battery, the same capacity as the A10's, and the A8's is removable, so a charged spare can take over mid shift. The A6 has 5050mAh, smaller than the A8's, and it is removable too. Capacity matters most in the cold, when any lithium battery delivers less.

Our cold weather guide explains why a tablet showing 40% on a frosty morning is not necessarily a faulty battery. For topping up between jobs, the 12V DC Car Charger on our accessories page is £26 and fits every device in the range.

GPS and Mapping

Mapping is where a tablet can earn its place for a landscaper, with the right app: measuring a lawn, walking a boundary, marking where the drains run. Both the A6 and the A8 list GPS, GLONASS, Galileo and BeiDou. Neither device lists a positioning accuracy, so treat any area or distance figure as a rough guide and use a proper survey where a boundary is in dispute.

A note on apps. Measuring, mapping, quoting and job management apps are all third party software. The A8 runs Android 12 and the A6 Android 15. Android 12 is the older release, so newer apps are more likely to drop support for it first. Either way, check that the specific app you rely on runs on the device, and works at that screen size, before you commit.

Both have 4G LTE with dual SIM; check your network's coverage map for the areas you work in.

Camera

Before and after photos sell the next job and settle the odd dispute about what the client asked for. Both have a 13MP rear camera with flash and a 5MP front camera, and the A8's rear camera is listed as autofocus. For quoting and record keeping either does the job.

Drops and Cold

The A6 lists a 1.5 metre drop rating and operating temperatures from minus 20°C to 50°C. The A8 lists neither a drop rating nor an operating temperature range, so if you crouch, kneel and work through frosty mornings, the A6 is the one with the figures behind it. If you want a tablet with a listed rugged test, the A10 is rated MIL-STD-810H and from minus 20°C to 60°C. Our MIL-STD-810H guide explains what that rating does and does not tell you. No rating is a guarantee, and a hard landing on a patio slab is still a hard landing.

Quoting on Site

One practical gain for a small landscaping firm is doing the quote on the spot: walk the site, measure it, photograph it, price it and email it before you leave. That is easier on an 8 inch screen than on a phone, and, if your quoting app supports it, the client can see a sketch or a plant list and sign on the screen. A Hand Strap for the A8 is £24 on the accessories page, and a Capacitive Stylus for signatures is £14.99. Note that the stylus is listed for the A8, the A10 and the Windows range, not the A6.

For maintenance rounds, the quote is usually a number and a sentence, and the A6 handles that from a pocket.

Our Picks for Landscaping and Garden Work

Tuga A8: For Quoting, Plans and Mapping

The Tuga A8 suits a landscaper who designs, quotes and plans on site and keeps the tablet in the van between jobs.

  • 8 inch IPS screen with AGC glass, 1280 x 800, 1000 nits
  • IP67
  • 8000mAh removable battery
  • 4G LTE dual SIM, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, NFC, GPS, GLONASS, Galileo and BeiDou
  • 13MP autofocus rear camera with flash, 5MP front camera
  • 6GB RAM, 128GB storage, microSD slot
  • Android 12
  • VESA mount points: the Vehicle Mounting Dock is £109
  • £379

Where it falls short: IP67 does not cover the pressure washer, so wipe it down instead. It runs Android 12, older than the A6's Android 15, and no drop rating, weight or operating temperature is listed for it. And it is a tablet, not a pocket device.

Tuga A6: For the Pocket

The Tuga A6 is a 6 inch handheld rather than a tablet. It suits garden maintenance rounds and grounds teams, where the device spends the day in a pocket or holster and comes out for a quick photo, a note or a job sign-off.

  • 6 inch FHD+ IPS screen, 2160 x 1080
  • IP67, rated for 1.5 metre drops
  • 5050mAh removable battery
  • 4G LTE dual SIM, dual-band Wi-Fi 5, Bluetooth 5.1, NFC, GPS, GLONASS, BeiDou and Galileo
  • Built-in 2D barcode scanner with two side scan keys
  • 13MP rear camera with flash, 5MP front camera
  • 4GB RAM, 64GB storage, microSD up to 256GB
  • 277g, Android 15
  • £349

Where it falls short: the screen and the battery. At 6 inches it is phone sized, and showing a client a planting plan on it means pinching and zooming. The 5050mAh battery is smaller than the A8's 8000mAh, so on a long day you will want a spare or the car charger. It lists no fingerprint sensor, so set a PIN you can type with dirty hands. The barcode scanner is useful if you track plant stock or tagged equipment, and costs you nothing if you do not. The Belt Holster (£22) carries it on your belt and the Car Phone Mount (£17) holds it in the vehicle, both on the accessories page.

Which One Should You Buy?

It comes down to two questions: does it need to fit in a pocket, and do you need to show people things on it? Neither device should be pressure washed.

  • Design and build landscaper, quotes with drawings, one device in the van: the A8.
  • Garden maintenance, mowing rounds, grounds crews, device lives in a pocket: the A6.
  • A crew: an A6 each for the crew and an A8 for whoever quotes. The A8 is £30 more than the A6.
  • Detailed garden design drawings: the A10 at £449 has the Full HD 10.1 inch screen for that, but at 350 nits it belongs in the van or the office rather than out on the lawn.

When Something Else Is the Better Buy

If all you do is take photos, send a few messages and raise invoices from the van, a decent phone in a good case may be all you need, and you probably already own one. A rugged device makes sense when the phone is the thing that keeps breaking, or when you want a screen big enough to quote from.

If your garden design software only runs on a Windows PC, neither of these Android devices will run it. Our guide to Android or Windows rugged tablets walks through that decision. Our Windows 11 models are rated IP65 to IP67, with no IP69K, so the same rule applies: a Windows tablet and a pressure washer should keep their distance.
